tool.kick.countMovements: Counting kicks is optional. It's one way to get to know how your baby usually moves. What matters is noticing a change. If your baby moves less than usual, call that day, whatever this counter says.
tool.kick.goal: A common guide: 10 movements in 2 hours
tool.common.timeToGoToThe: 🚨 Time to go to the hospital
tool.feed.fewFeedsBody: Newborns typically need 8–12 feedings per 24 hours. If baby is difficult to wake or not gaining weight, call your doctor.
tool.diaper.day1212: Day 1–2: 1–2 wet diapers · Day 3–4: 3–4 wet · Day 5+: 6+ wet, 3–4 dirty per day. Fewer than 6 wet diapers after day 5 → call your doctor.
tool.jaundice.callImmediatelyIf: Call your doctor right away if
tool.jaundice.setBirthDateHint: Set baby birth date above to see day-by-day guidance, following AAP newborn jaundice guidance.
tool.jaundice.day1: First day. Bilirubin is being checked before hospital discharge. Baby is monitored by the nursing staff.
tool.jaundice.day2: Bilirubin levels are rising. Hospital checks before discharge. Watch for yellowing of skin and whites of eyes.
tool.jaundice.day3: Jaundice peaks around days 3–5 in most babies. Yellow color may be more visible. Feeding frequently (8–12 times/day) helps the body clear bilirubin.
tool.jaundice.day4: Peak jaundice period. Make sure baby is feeding well and having wet diapers. Your baby's doctor may want to see the baby around now.
tool.jaundice.day5: Visit with your baby's doctor: weight check + bilirubin level. Levels should start to level off. If baby is sleepy and not feeding, call your baby's doctor.
tool.jaundice.day6: Levels should start declining in full-term babies. Continue feeding frequently. If skin is deeply yellow or baby won't wake to feed. Call your doctor.
tool.jaundice.day7: Most term babies' jaundice is improving by now. Watch for yellowing spreading to legs and feet, which signals higher levels.
tool.jaundice.day10: In most term babies, jaundice is nearly resolved. If it's persisting or worsening, your doctor will want to check a bilirubin level.
tool.jaundice.day14: 2-week visit. Jaundice should be resolved in term babies. Persistent jaundice beyond 2 weeks may need further evaluation. Tell your doctor.
tool.jaundice.day21: Jaundice lasting beyond 3 weeks is considered prolonged and should be evaluated. Breastfed babies can have mild jaundice longer, but it still needs to be checked.
tool.jaundice.redFlags: Baby won't wake to feed · Deeply yellow skin spreading to legs · Arching back or high-pitched cry · White or gray stools · Very dark urine
tool.bp.anyReading14090During: ACOG counts any reading of 140/90 or higher in pregnancy or after birth as high. 160/110 or higher needs a call to L&D or 911 now. Home cuffs can read high, so one high reading means call and recheck, not panic.

tool.nausea.intro: Nausea is usually worse on an empty stomach, so small amounts often beat big meals. Tap each hour you ate or drank something. The point is not how much, it is how long the gaps are.
tool.nausea.tapHour: Tap an hour to mark that you ate
tool.nausea.gapOk: {hours} hours. Try to keep gaps under about 3 hours while you are awake.
tool.nausea.gapLong: {hours} hours. Long gaps make nausea worse. Try something small, even a few bites.
tool.nausea.weekPrompt: Enter the week of pregnancy you are in, so this can show you where you are.
tool.nausea.timelineLabel: Nausea timeline, you are at week {week}
tool.nausea.phaseEarly: Nausea often begins around week 6. If it has not started, it may not start at all.
tool.nausea.phasePeak: This is usually the hardest stretch. It tends to peak around weeks 9 to 10 and then ease.
tool.nausea.phaseEasing: For most women it starts easing from here. About 6 in 10 are past it by week 14.
tool.nausea.phaseMost: About 9 in 10 women are past the worst by week 22. If yours is not easing, tell your doctor.
tool.nausea.phaseLate: Nausea this late is less common. It is worth telling your doctor, who can look for other causes.
tool.nausea.flag.noFluids: You cannot keep any fluids down for a whole day
tool.nausea.flag.vomitingOften: You are vomiting several times a day, every day
tool.nausea.flag.weightLoss: You are losing weight instead of gaining
tool.nausea.flag.darkUrine: Your urine is dark, or you have not passed any for 8 hours
tool.nausea.flag.dizzy: You feel dizzy or faint when you stand up
tool.nausea.callTodayBody: Severe pregnancy sickness has a name, hyperemesis gravidarum, and it is treatable. The real danger is dehydration, not the nausea itself. Do not wait it out.
tool.nausea.strat.empty.name: Never let your stomach get empty
tool.nausea.strat.empty.how: Eat something small before you get hungry, and keep crackers by the bed for before you sit up.
tool.nausea.strat.bland.name: Bland, dry, cold food
tool.nausea.strat.bland.how: Cold food smells less. Dry toast, crackers, plain rice, cold fruit.
tool.nausea.strat.fluids.name: Sip fluids between meals
tool.nausea.strat.fluids.how: Drinking with food fills you up faster. Sip small amounts all day instead.
tool.nausea.strat.triggers.name: Learn your triggers
tool.nausea.strat.triggers.how: Smells are the usual culprit. Cooking, coffee, perfume. Let someone else cook if you can.
tool.nausea.strat.b6.name: Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine)
tool.nausea.strat.b6.how: 10 to 25 mg, three or four times a day. No more than 200 mg in 24 hours. Sold over the counter.
tool.nausea.strat.ginger.name: Ginger
tool.nausea.strat.ginger.how: Tea, capsules, or chews. Modest evidence, and it helps some women a lot.
tool.nausea.strat.acupressure.name: Wrist pressure
tool.nausea.strat.acupressure.how: Pressing the P6 point, or a wristband. See the instructions below.
tool.nausea.strat.vitamin.name: Move your prenatal vitamin
tool.nausea.strat.vitamin.how: Iron is a common culprit. Take it at night, or with food. Ask about a low-iron option.
tool.nausea.strat.rest.name: Rest, and get up slowly
tool.nausea.strat.rest.how: Tiredness makes nausea worse. Sit on the edge of the bed a moment before standing.
tool.nausea.strat.doxylamine.name: Doxylamine, added to B6
tool.nausea.strat.doxylamine.how: 12.5 mg at bedtime, which is half a 25 mg Unisom SleepTab. If that is not enough your doctor may add a morning and afternoon dose. No more than 50 mg in 24 hours. Buy SleepTabs, not SleepGels: SleepGels are a different drug. No prescription needed.
tool.nausea.triedAll: You have marked everything as tried. If nothing is helping, that is worth a call.
tool.nausea.stratNote: Tap anything you have tried to keep track. Ask your doctor before starting a supplement or medicine.
tool.nausea.howIsItNow: How is the nausea right now?
tool.nausea.lowerIsBetter: Lower is better. This is only your own record, not medical proof.
tool.nausea.noEntries: No entries yet. Log how you feel a few times and this will show what helps you.
tool.nausea.acuIntro: Evidence is mixed, but it costs nothing, has no side effects, and helps some women. Worth ten minutes to find out.
tool.nausea.acuBands: Elastic wristbands with a plastic stud, sold for travel sickness, press the same point. Wear one on each wrist.
tool.nausea.acu.find: Turn one hand palm up, fingers relaxed.
tool.nausea.acu.measure: Lay three fingers of your other hand across the wrist, with the finger nearest your hand sitting on the crease where your hand meets your arm.
tool.nausea.acu.feel: The point is just past your third finger, in the middle of the wrist. Press around and you should feel two firm cords running down the arm. The point sits between them.
tool.nausea.acu.press: Press firmly with your thumb, hard enough to feel it but not to hurt. Small circles or steady pressure, for two to three minutes.
tool.nausea.acu.both: Do the same on the other wrist. Repeat whenever the nausea rises.
tool.nausea.logIntro: Rate the nausea whenever it changes. After a few entries this will show which of the things you tried actually helped you.

usNotice.title: Care in the United States
usNotice.body: Obiana follows prenatal care in the United States. Visits, tests and advice in other countries can be different.
about.privacyOnDevice: What you type stays on this phone. No account, no sign-in, nothing sent. Clearing your browser data erases it, so use Export to keep a copy.
about.privacySubmit: Only two buttons send anything: Help translate and Help Improve This Guide. They send what you wrote, your country, and a scrambled network address to stop spam. Never your name or what is in your trackers.
disclaimer.title: Before you start
disclaimer.education: This is general information, not medical advice. Ask your family doctor, OB or midwife about your own pregnancy.
disclaimer.tools: The trackers keep what you type. They can't diagnose anything.
today.savedOnPhone: This stays on your phone. You can change it any time under Me.
urgent.title: When to call
urgent.addLd: Add your labor & delivery number under Me.
urgent.tellThem: If you had a baby in the last year, tell anyone you call or see. Some serious problems after birth are missed when staff don't know.
urgent.line988: Thoughts of harming yourself, or in crisis: call or text 988, the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline.
urgent.lineMama: Feeling low, anxious or overwhelmed, in pregnancy or after: National Maternal Mental Health Hotline, 1-833-TLC-MAMA (1-833-852-6262). Call or text. Interpreters in many languages.
urgent.linePoison: Swallowed something, you or the baby: Poison Control, 1-800-222-1222.
urgent.lineDv: Not safe at home: National Domestic Violence Hotline, 1-800-799-7233, or text START to 88788.
visits.title: Your visits, week by week
visits.sub: What happens at each visit, and what's up to you
visits.lead: This is the usual US schedule. Yours may be different: your family doctor, OB or midwife adds visits and tests when you need them.
visits.first.title: First visit
visits.first.i1: Your due date is set from your last period, often with an early ultrasound.
visits.first.i2: Blood tests: blood type and Rh, blood count, immunity to rubella and chickenpox, hepatitis B and C, HIV and syphilis. A urine test, and tests for chlamydia and gonorrhea.
visits.first.i3: An early sugar test if you had diabetes in a past pregnancy or have other risk factors.
visits.first.i4: If you are at higher risk of preeclampsia, low-dose aspirin (81 mg a day) from 12 weeks lowers that risk. Ask if it's right for you.
visits.genetic.title: Tests for the baby
visits.genetic.i1: A blood test from 10 weeks (cell-free DNA) screens for Down syndrome and a few other conditions. A screen is not a diagnosis: a positive result means a diagnostic test is offered.
visits.genetic.i2: Carrier screening checks whether you carry genes for conditions such as cystic fibrosis or spinal muscular atrophy.
visits.genetic.i3: You can have all, some or none of these.
visits.monthly.title: Regular visits
visits.monthly.i1: Blood pressure, weight, urine and the baby's heartbeat. From about 20 weeks, the size of your belly is measured too.
visits.anatomy.title: Anatomy ultrasound
visits.anatomy.i1: A detailed scan of the baby's body, growth and the placenta. You can usually learn the sex, if you want to.
visits.sugar.title: Sugar test and blood work
visits.sugar.i1: A sweet drink, then a blood test an hour later, checks for gestational diabetes.
visits.sugar.i2: A blood count for anemia, and a repeat syphilis test.
visits.sugar.i3: If your blood type is Rh negative: an Rh shot (RhoGAM) at about 28 weeks.
visits.tdap.title: Whooping cough shot (Tdap)
visits.tdap.i1: Your antibodies pass to the baby and protect them in the first months, before they can have their own shots. You get it in every pregnancy.
visits.twoweekly.title: Visits get closer
visits.twoweekly.i1: Get to know how your baby usually moves. Counting kicks is optional. If the baby moves less than usual, call that day. Don't wait for the next visit.
visits.twoweekly.i2: If you have a condition such as high blood pressure or diabetes, extra checks of the baby (non-stress tests or ultrasounds) often start around 32 weeks.
visits.rsv.title: RSV protection for the baby
visits.rsv.i1: Either an RSV vaccine for you at 32 to 36 weeks, or an antibody shot for the baby after birth. One or the other, not both. Each lowers the chance that the baby ends up in the hospital with RSV in their first winter.
visits.gbs.title: Group B strep swab, and the baby's position
visits.gbs.i1: A swab of the vagina and rectum. About 1 in 4 women carry GBS, and it does not harm you. If yours is positive, you get IV antibiotics in labor to protect the baby.
visits.gbs.i2: A check that the baby is head down. If the baby is bottom first (breech), you may be offered a way to turn the baby (external cephalic version), or you can plan a C-section.
visits.gbs.i3: Go over your birth plan: pain relief, who will be with you, feeding.
visits.weekly.title: The last weeks
visits.weekly.i1: From 38 weeks you may be offered a membrane sweep: a finger sweep at the cervix that can help labor start.
visits.weekly.i2: Induction can be offered from 39 weeks. By 41 weeks it is recommended, because the risk to the baby starts to rise.
visits.ppBp.title: Blood pressure check, if yours was high
visits.ppBp.i1: If you had high blood pressure or preeclampsia, have it checked within 3 to 10 days of the birth. Preeclampsia can start or get worse after delivery.
visits.pp3.title: First check-in
visits.pp3.i1: Talk to your family doctor, OB or midwife about bleeding, pain, feeding, mood and sleep. A phone or video call can count.
visits.ppFull.when: By 12 weeks after birth, often at 4–6
visits.ppFull.title: Full postpartum visit
visits.ppFull.i1: A mood check, birth control, how you are healing, and any plans for a next pregnancy.
visits.ppFull.i2: If you had gestational diabetes: a sugar test 4 to 12 weeks after birth. The risk of type 2 diabetes stays higher for life, so ask for a check every 1 to 3 years.
visits.ppFull.i3: If you leak urine or stool, have pain with sex, or feel a bulge in the vagina, ask about pelvic floor physical therapy. It helps. You don't have to live with it.
